Sri Lanka's maternal mortality rate is in the same range as Western Europe's.

Its neighbor Afghanistan's is roughly 25x higher.

Sri Lanka only became upper-middle-income in the last couple of years. It built this outcome while poor.

a thread 🧵🗺️ Data: Our World in Data (CC BY)

1/ Maternal death is usually one of the tightest correlates of national income anywhere in health data. Rich countries lose almost no mothers in childbirth; the poorest lose over 1,000 per 100,000 births. Sri Lanka breaks that curve badly.

2/ It starts in 1879, when a Ceylonese businessman, Charles Henry de Soysa, funded a maternity home in Colombo. In 1881 it opened the island's first school training midwives as licensed professionals, not informal helpers.

3/ The colonial and post-independence state kept building on that instinct: public health units nationwide by 1952, then a free health system after 1948 that put a trained midwife within reach of nearly every village, not just city hospitals.

4/ One estimate puts Sri Lanka's maternal mortality ratio at roughly 2,100 per 100,000 births in 1881. By the mid-1990s it was around 24. It kept falling through a civil war, coups and currency crises.

5/ The model: a midwife for a defined set of households, a small local maternity home for routine births, a hospital for real emergencies. Three tiers, each doing only its job — and a World Bank study found the same pattern in Malaysia, the other big overachiever.

6/ Even the 2022 economic collapse — default, fuel shortages, medicine shortages — didn't unravel this. Ratios ticked up but didn't crash back toward regional norms. A system built on midwives and local clinics is hard to break all at once.
